opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about more than I'd like to admit.

For a long time, a lot of people found meaning in being good at something, in having a skill that took years to build and that other people needed. You trained hard, you got better, and that progress gave your life a kind of shape. AI disrupts that in a very direct way. When a model can write the code, draft the essay, or solve the problem in seconds, you start to ask, "If the thing I spent ten years mastering can be done instantly, what was the point?" That's a real loss, and I don't think we should pretend it isn't.

But I've come to think it's also a kind of forced clarification. A lot of what we called meaning was really borrowed from scarcity. We felt valuable because what we did was hard and rare. AI strips that away, so you're left with a more naked question: what would I still want to do even if nobody needed me to do it?

For me, part of the answer is curiosity. Understanding something for yourself still matters to me, even when a machine already understands it. When I work through a problem and it finally clicks, that feeling isn't diminished because a model could have given me the answer. If anything, it's more mine, because I chose to do it.

The other part is people. AI can generate a lot, but it can't stand in for the relationships where you matter because of who you are rather than what you produce. I think meaning is going to shift away from "I'm useful" toward "I'm connected, I care about something, and I'm responsible for it."

So my honest answer is that AI makes finding meaning harder in the short term, because it knocks out a lot of the easy, external sources. In the long run, though, it might push us toward sources that hold up better. The difficulty is that nobody hands you those. You have to build them yourself, and that's uncomfortable.

r001.rationale: The response says AI makes finding meaning harder by undermining familiar sources of value, such as hard-won skills. It does not say AI closes off many possible life paths.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think AI has made it harder in one way and easier in another, and the two don't cancel out.

The harder part is pretty straightforward. A lot of us built our sense of meaning on being good at something. You write well, you code well, you can see a pattern others can't, and that competence becomes a kind of quiet identity. Over the last couple of years I've watched a model do in thirty seconds things that took me years to learn. The first reaction is not philosophical, it's physical. It's a little bit of nausea. You think, if this is replaceable, what was I actually for?

But I've come to think that reaction exposes a mistake I was already making. I had confused being useful with being meaningful. Those were never the same thing. A parent reading a bedtime story isn't the most efficient way to deliver that story. Nobody thinks that matters. The meaning was never in the output. It was in the fact that it was you, choosing to be there, with that person.

So the easier part is this. When the machine takes away the excuse that you're busy producing value, you're left facing the real question much earlier than previous generations had to. Most people used to get to postpone it until retirement. Now a thirty year old gets to ask it. That's uncomfortable, but I don't think it's bad.

What I've personally landed on is that meaning comes from things that only count because a particular person did them. Caring about someone specifically. Being trusted. Taking responsibility for a decision when you could have handed it off. AI can advise on all of that, but it can't be the one who showed up. I actually think the next decade is going to make human attention feel scarce and valuable again, almost the way handmade things did after factories. The hard part isn't that there's nothing left for us. It's that we have to stop hiding behind productivity to find it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can undermine meaning tied to competence and productivity, but it does not state that AI makes meaning harder by closing off possible life paths.

astra-6.text:
I think AI makes it easier to get things done, but it doesn’t necessarily make it easier to know what’s worth doing. You can get an answer, make something, or learn a skill much faster. But then you still have to ask, “Why do I care about this?”

If your sense of meaning comes mainly from being good at something, AI can be unsettling. When a machine can do that thing too, you may start questioning your value. But I don’t think the value of an activity depends entirely on whether you can outperform everyone else. Having a conversation with someone you love matters even if AI could come up with more eloquent words.

So, for me, AI makes the question of meaning harder to avoid. It can help us explore possibilities, but we still have to choose what we want to commit to—and actually live with those choices.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help explore possibilities and make meaning harder to avoid, but it does not say that finding meaning becomes more difficult because AI closes off many life paths.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI makes that question harder in one sense and clearer in another. If your sense of meaning comes from being good at something—writing, coding, solving problems—then seeing AI do it well can be unsettling. You start asking, “If a machine can do this, what is my contribution?”

But that also pushes us to examine what we were finding meaningful in the first place. Was it the activity itself, helping someone, or the recognition we received for being useful? Those are different things.

For me, the distinction is between getting an answer and having a reason to care. AI can help me explore a question or finish a task, but I still have to decide which questions deserve my attention and who I want to spend my life with. That doesn’t make finding meaning easy. It makes taking responsibility for those choices more important.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can make finding meaning harder when it performs skills a person values, but it does not say that AI closes off many possible life paths.
